units.title: Your first scene
units.blurb: What Three.js is; scene, camera, renderer and Mesh; the animation loop and window resizing.

lessons.title: What is Three.js
lessons.sub: 3D in the browser without the WebGL pain

cards.title: 3D right on the page
cards.body:
Browsers can draw 3D through WebGL, which gives JavaScript access to the GPU. But WebGL is very low-level: shaders, buffers, matrices. Drawing a single cube takes about a hundred lines.

Three.js is a library on top of WebGL. You say "here is a scene, here is a camera, here is a cube", and it does all the low-level work.

cards.title: Four key words
cards.body:
Scene: everything that exists in the world.
Camera: where we look from and how.
Renderer: the artist. It takes the scene and the camera and paints a picture on a canvas.
Mesh: a visible object, made of a geometry (the shape) plus a material (how the surface looks).

cards.q: Match them up
Why use Three.js if the browser already has WebGL?
options: WebGL is too low-level: Three.js handles the shaders, buffers and matrices for you
Without Three.js the browser cannot do 3D
cards.explain: Three.js is WebGL (and now WebGPU too), just pleasant to use.

cards.title: Where you will see it
cards.body:
Product configurators ("design your sneakers"), 3D model and BIM viewers in the browser, data visualization, portfolio sites with effects, browser games.

It was created by Ricardo Cabello (mrdoob), and the first version came out in 2010. Versions are named by release number: r170, r171…

cards.title: How to add it
cards.body: In a project with a bundler (Vite, webpack): npm install three. Without a bundler, load the module from a CDN through an import map.

cards.q: Import Three.js
cards.code: import * as ___ from '___';
cards.explain: The package is called three, and by convention everything goes into an object named THREE.

cards.q: What do you need to see a cube? Select all that apply.
cards.explain: Three.js runs entirely in the browser. A server is only needed to serve the files.

cards.title: The smallest program
cards.body: Create a scene, a camera and a renderer, make a cube, put it in the scene and ask the renderer to draw.

cards.task: The screen is empty. Turn on lines of code until the cube shows up. Above is real Three.js.

cards.q: Why is the cube invisible when camera.position.z = 0?
options: The camera is inside the cube: from inside, the faces point away from us and are not drawn
cards.explain: Both the camera and the cube start at (0, 0, 0). That is why you move the camera back.

cards.title: Where the camera looks
cards.body: By default the camera sits at the origin and looks down the −Z axis, "into the screen". So you move it back along +Z: camera.position.z = 5. Y points up, X points right.

cards.q: Put the steps in order
items: Create the camera and move it back
Create the renderer and add its canvas to the page
Create a Mesh and add it to the scene
cards.explain: The creation order matters less than calling render once everything is ready.

cards.q: Which line keeps the cube from showing up?
cards.explain: The cube is created but never added to the scene: scene.add(cube) is missing. The renderer only draws the scene.

cards.q: A Mesh from a geometry and a material
cards.explain: Three.js has no Cube class. A cube is a Mesh with a BoxGeometry.

cards.q: Match them up
pairs: Colors by face direction, needs no light
The canvas element for the page
Put an object into the world

cards.q: Where does a Three.js camera look by default?
cards.explain: To look at a specific point, use camera.lookAt(x, y, z).

cards.title: A picture is drawn once
cards.body: renderer.render draws a single frame. To make things move, you have to keep drawing frames, about 60 times a second, and change the scene in between.

cards.task: The cube is standing still. Make it spin.

cards.q: Why is setAnimationLoop better than your own while(true) loop?
options: The browser calls your function before each screen frame and the page does not freeze
cards.explain: Under the hood it uses requestAnimationFrame, and you also need it for VR/AR sessions.

cards.title: Speed should not depend on the monitor
cards.body: With += 0.01 per frame, the cube spins more than twice as fast on a 144 Hz monitor as on a 60 Hz one. The right way is to multiply by the time since the last frame.

cards.q: On a teammate's 120 Hz monitor the cube spins twice as fast. Why?
options: Rotation is added per frame, not per second, and they get twice as many frames
cards.explain: Multiply the speed by dt from THREE.Clock.

cards.title: The window was resized
cards.body: When the window size changes, update both the camera and the renderer. Otherwise the picture gets stretched.

cards.q: The window got wider and the cube looks squashed. Tap the line that should be followed by one more call.
cards.explain: After changing aspect (or fov, near, far) you need camera.updateProjectionMatrix(). Otherwise the camera keeps using the old values.

cards.q: Why Math.min(devicePixelRatio, 2)?
options: On a screen with pixel ratio 3 you would render 9 times as many pixels, which is heavy for a phone
It does not work without it
cards.explain: A ratio of 2 already looks sharp, and the cost grows with the square.

cards.q: Match them up

lessons.title: Final: your first scene
lessons.sub: From an empty canvas to a spinning cube

cards.task: Build a spinning cube from scratch.

cards.q: After which line did someone forget to add the canvas to the page?
cards.explain: The renderer.domElement canvas never got onto the page: document.body.appendChild(renderer.domElement).

cards.q: Why might the screen be empty? Select all that apply.
options: The Mesh was not added to the scene
The camera is inside the object
The camera was moved back along +Z
cards.explain: Moving the camera back along +Z is exactly the right thing to do.

cards.q: What does cube.rotation.y += 1.5 * dt do?
options: Rotates 1.5 radians per second at any frame rate
cards.explain: Radians, not degrees. A full turn is 2π ≈ 6.28.

cards.q: The resize handler
cards.explain: Camera first, then the canvas.

cards.q: Match them up
pairs: A friendly library on top of it

cards.q: Spinning in a loop
cards.explain: Without render inside the loop, the scene would change but no frames would be drawn.

cards.q: What does renderer.render(scene, camera) draw?
options: One frame: the scene as seen by this camera
cards.explain: For animation, call render every frame.

units.title: The camera
units.blurb: PerspectiveCamera: fov, aspect, near and far; z-fighting, lookAt and OrbitControls; OrthographicCamera.

lessons.title: PerspectiveCamera
lessons.sub: Field of view, aspect, near and far

cards.title: The view pyramid
cards.body:
A camera sees a truncated pyramid called the frustum. Four numbers define it:

fov: the vertical field of view in degrees.
aspect: frame width ÷ height.
near: nothing closer than this is drawn.
far: nothing farther than this is drawn either.
cards.code: new THREE.PerspectiveCamera(fov, aspect, near, far);

cards.task: The green cube sits off to the side and is out of frame. Widen the view without moving the camera.

cards.q: What does a large fov, say 100, do?
options: You see more, but objects get smaller and the edges distort, like a wide-angle lens
cards.explain: Typical scenes use 40–75.

cards.task: The blue cube is far away and has disappeared. Fix it without touching fov or the camera position.

cards.q: Why did the blue cube disappear?
options: It is 20 units away and far = 10: anything beyond far gets cut off
cards.explain: far is the back wall of the view frustum.

cards.title: Units
cards.body: Three.js has no built-in units: 1 is just 1. But glTF and physics engines agree that 1 = 1 meter, and it pays to stick with that: lights and shadows are tuned for that scale.

cards.q: Match each parameter to its meaning
A camera with a 60° angle that sees from 0.1 to 1000
cards.code: new THREE.PerspectiveCamera(___, w / h, ___, 1000);
cards.explain: near = 0 is not allowed. More on that in the next lesson.

cards.q: The fov of a PerspectiveCamera is the angle…
cards.explain: The horizontal angle is derived from the vertical one and aspect.

lessons.title: near, lookAt and OrbitControls
lessons.sub: How not to clip nearby objects, and how to let users orbit the scene

cards.task: The red cube is right next to the camera, but you cannot see it. Fix it.

cards.title: Why not set near = 0.000001
cards.body:
Each pixel's depth is stored with limited precision, and almost all of it is spent on the area close to near. Make near too small and distant surfaces start to flicker, showing through each other. This is z-fighting.

The rule: near as large as possible, far as small as possible, as long as the scene still fits.

cards.q: Distant walls flicker and "bleed" through each other. What do you check first?
options: Whether near is too small (and far too large)
cards.explain: The classic cause of z-fighting is near = 0.0001 with far = 100000.

cards.task: The blue cube should NOT be drawn (it is background and just gets in the way), but red and green should.

cards.title: lookAt
cards.body: You can put the camera anywhere and turn it toward a point: camera.lookAt(x, y, z).
cards.code:
camera.position.set(4, 3, 6);
camera.lookAt(0, 0, 0);

cards.title: OrbitControls: spin it with the mouse
cards.body: A ready-made add-on: dragging orbits the camera around a target, the wheel zooms. With enableDamping the motion is smooth, and then you need controls.update() in the loop.

cards.q: You turned on enableDamping and the camera jerks around. Before which line does controls.update() belong?
cards.explain: controls.update() goes before render. It is what produces the smooth easing.

cards.q: Match them up
pairs: Turn the camera toward a point

cards.q: Where to import OrbitControls from
cards.code: import { OrbitControls } from 'three/___/controls/OrbitControls.js';
cards.explain: three/addons/ is the short path to the examples and add-ons shipped in the three package.

cards.title: Distant things do not shrink
cards.body:
An OrthographicCamera has no perspective: objects of the same size look the same up close and far away. The view pyramid becomes a box.

It is used for technical drawings and CAD views, isometric games, and 2D interfaces on top of 3D.
cards.code:
const h = 10, w = h * aspect;
const camera = new THREE.OrthographicCamera(-w / 2, w / 2, h / 2, -h / 2, 0.1, 100);

cards.q: Two identical cubes: one 2 meters away, the other 20. How do they look through an OrthographicCamera?
options: The far one is 10 times smaller
cards.explain: Perspective shrinking only happens with a PerspectiveCamera.

cards.title: Six numbers instead of fov
cards.body: left, right, top, bottom are the box edges in scene units, and near, far work as before. To zoom, use the zoom property (and call updateProjectionMatrix() again after changing it).

cards.q: Where does an OrthographicCamera make sense? Select all that apply.
options: A part drawing with exact dimensions
cards.explain: A "living" first-person view needs perspective.

cards.q: The window got wider and the picture stretched. Which line in resize needs fixing?
cards.explain: The edges must depend on the aspect ratio: camera.left = -w / 2; camera.right = w / 2.

cards.q: Match them up
pairs: Like an eye: far things look smaller
Like a blueprint: sizes stay the same

cards.q: What do both cameras have in common?
options: near, far, and the need to call updateProjectionMatrix after changes
cards.explain: Only the perspective camera has fov.

cards.q: Zoom the ortho camera in 2x
cards.code:
camera.___ = 2;
camera.___();
cards.explain: An ortho camera has no fov, so you zoom with zoom.

cards.task: Everything is broken: the angle is too narrow, near is too far away and far is too close. Make all three cubes visible.

cards.q: You set camera.fov = 75 and nothing changed. Why?
options: You have to recreate the renderer
cards.explain: The camera caches its projection matrix.

cards.q: What will cut an object out of the picture? Select all that apply.
options: It is outside the field of view
cards.explain: A dark object is still drawn, just dark.

cards.q: Place the camera and turn it toward the center
cards.code:
camera.position.set(4, 3, 6);
camera.___(0, 0, 0);
cards.explain: lookAt turns an object to face a point.

cards.q: Match the symptom to the cause
Which camera fits an isometric game?
cards.explain: Isometric means no perspective shrinking.

cards.q: OrbitControls with enableDamping. What must be in the loop?
cards.explain: Calling update every frame smoothly finishes the motion.

cards.task: Keep only red and green in the frame: blue is background and should not be drawn. Do not touch fov or the camera.

units.title: Objects in the scene
units.blurb: position, rotation in radians and scale; axes; hierarchy with Group, local and world coordinates.

lessons.title: position, rotation, scale
lessons.sub: Where an object is, how it is turned and how big it is

cards.title: Three properties of every object
cards.body:
Every object in the scene (a Mesh, a camera, a light, a group) has:

position: where it is, as x, y, z.
rotation: rotation around the X, Y, Z axes, in radians.
scale: size along each axis, where 1 is the original size.

cards.q: cube.rotation.y = 90: how far does the cube turn?
options: 90 radians, which is more than 14 full turns, not 90°
cards.explain: You need Math.PI / 2 or THREE.MathUtils.degToRad(90).

cards.q: Rotate 180° around Y
cards.code: mesh.rotation.y = Math.___;
cards.explain: π radians = 180°.

cards.title: Axes in Three.js
cards.body: Y is up, X is right, Z points toward the viewer. It is a right-handed coordinate system, the same as glTF. In Blender and many CAD tools Z is up, which is why imported models sometimes end up "lying down".

cards.q: Match them up
A model from Blender is lying on its side. Likely cause?
options: In Blender Z is up, in Three.js it is Y
cards.explain: Blender's glTF exporter usually converts the axes for you (+Y Up). Check that option.

cards.q: Which objects have position, rotation and scale? Select all that apply.
cards.explain: All of these inherit from Object3D. A material is not a scene object.

cards.q: What does THREE.MathUtils.degToRad(180) return?
cards.explain: π.

cards.title: Objects inside objects
cards.body:
Any object can be a parent: earth.add(moon). A child's position is measured from its parent: a Moon at x = 1.2 is 1.2 from the Earth, not from the center of the world.

Move, rotate or scale the parent, and the children go along with it.

cards.title: An empty parent: Group
cards.body: THREE.Group is an invisible holder object. Take a solar system: the Earth sits inside a "pivot" group, 4 units from the center. Rotate the pivot and the Earth travels along its orbit.

cards.task: The Moon should travel with the Earth. Pick the right parent for it and take two orbit steps.

cards.q: Why did the Moon stay put with scene.add(moon)?
options: Its parent is the scene, and the scene does not rotate; the Earth's pivot has nothing to do with it
cards.explain: Motion is passed only down the chain from parent to children.

cards.task: Make the Earth twice as big and take one orbit step. What happened to the Moon?

cards.q: Why did the Moon move out to 2.4 and grow too?
options: A parent's scale applies to everything inside it: both the size and the position of its children
cards.explain: To grow only the Earth, scale it in a separate group with no children.

cards.title: Where the object really is
cards.body: moon.position is the local position relative to the parent. To get the world position, ask like this:
cards.code:
const p = new THREE.Vector3();
moon.getWorldPosition(p);   // coordinates in the world

cards.q: Match them up
What does a child inherit from its parent? Select all that apply.
cards.explain: Each Mesh has its own material.

cards.task: Make the Earth twice as big, and let the Moon travel alongside it at a distance of 2.4. Three orbit steps.

cards.q: What do you write to rotate by 30°?
cards.explain: The third option converts in the opposite direction.

cards.q: A car wheel should turn along with the car. Which line gets in the way?
cards.explain: The wheel lives in the scene, not in the car. You need car.add(wheel).

cards.q: Make the Moon a satellite of the Earth
cards.code:
earth.___(moon);
moon.position.x = 1.2;
cards.explain: attach exists too: it keeps the world position when the parent changes. Here you want add.

cards.q: Match them up
Which are true? Select all that apply.
options: A child's position is measured from its parent
A parent's scale also stretches the distances to its children
cards.explain: Scene is an Object3D too, so it does have a position.

cards.q: How do you build a solar system where the Earth moves in a circle?
options: Put the Earth in a Group at the center, 4 units out, and rotate the group
Set x and z by hand every frame with sin and cos; it is the only way
cards.explain: sin/cos works too, but a group is simpler, and the Earth's children come along for the ride.

cards.task: Fix the system: the Moon stays put while the Earth flies away. Two orbit steps.

units.title: Lights and materials
units.blurb: Basic, Lambert and Standard; light sources and their falloff; the four shadow flags.

lessons.title: Materials
lessons.sub: Basic, Lambert, Standard, and why everything is black

cards.title: A material is how a surface looks
cards.body:
MeshBasicMaterial: a flat fill that ignores light.
MeshLambertMaterial: matte, cheap, reacts to light.
MeshStandardMaterial: physically based (PBR), with roughness and metalness. The de facto standard, same as in glTF.

cards.task: MeshStandardMaterial, yet all you see is a black silhouette. Fix it with light.

cards.q: Why is MeshStandardMaterial black without light?
options: It computes how much light the surface reflects; no light, nothing to reflect
cards.explain: The most common beginner mistake: "I see nothing" even though the camera is fine.

cards.task: There is light, but the knot looks flat, with no depth. Change the material.

cards.title: roughness and metalness
cards.body:
roughness: 0 is mirror smooth, 1 is matte (the default is 1).
metalness: 0 is plastic, wood, stone; 1 is metal.

Metal needs something to reflect: without an environment map (scene.environment) it looks dark. That is an intermediate-level topic.
cards.code: new THREE.MeshStandardMaterial({ color: 0x4f9dff, roughness: 0.3, metalness: 0 });

cards.q: Match each material to its use
Which materials react to light? Select all that apply.
cards.explain: Physical is an extended Standard: clearcoat, glass, fabric.

cards.q: Matte plastic
cards.code: new THREE.MeshStandardMaterial({ color: 0xff0000, ___: 0.9, ___: 0 });
cards.explain: shininess belongs to Phong, not Standard.

lessons.title: Lights
lessons.sub: Ambient, Directional, Point: how each one shines

cards.title: The main four
cards.body:
AmbientLight: even light from everywhere. It adds no depth, it just "lifts the shadows".
DirectionalLight: like the sun, parallel rays from one side.
PointLight: a light bulb, shining in all directions and fading with distance.
SpotLight: a spotlight, shining in a cone.

cards.task: Only an AmbientLight, so the knot looks flat. Add a bulb to bring out the shape.

cards.q: Why does the shape look flat with just an AmbientLight?
options: It shines equally from every side, so there are no lit and dark sides
It does not work with Standard
cards.explain: The eye reads shape from differences in lighting.

cards.title: Brightness in physical units
cards.body: Since r155, lighting in Three.js is physically correct. PointLight and SpotLight have decay = 2: brightness drops with the square of the distance. So a bulb with intensity = 1 five meters from an object barely lights it, and people use values in the tens.

cards.q: A PointLight with intensity 1 barely lights an object 5 meters away. Why?
options: Light fades with distance squared: at 5 m it is 25 times weaker
PointLight does not reach beyond 1 m
cards.explain: Raise the intensity or move the light closer.

cards.title: Where a DirectionalLight points
cards.body: A directional light shines from its position toward its target (the world origin by default). You can move the target, but then you have to add it to the scene.

cards.q: Match each light to its real-world twin
A classic, inexpensive lighting setup? Select everything it needs.
options: A dimmer AmbientLight or HemisphereLight, so shadows are not pitch black
One DirectionalLight as the key light
cards.explain: Every light is extra shader work for every pixel.

lessons.title: Shadows
lessons.sub: Four flags and one shadow map

cards.title: Shadows are off by default
cards.body: Shadows are expensive, so Three.js only draws them when you ask explicitly. You need all four settings:
cards.code:
renderer.shadowMap.enabled = true;   // the renderer supports shadows
sun.castShadow = true;               // the light casts shadows
knot.castShadow = true;              // the object casts them
floor.receiveShadow = true;          // the floor receives them

cards.task: The sun is shining, but there is no shadow on the floor. Turn on everything it takes.

cards.q: You set castShadow on the object and the light, and receiveShadow on the floor, but there is no shadow. What did you forget?
options: Shadows only work with an OrthographicCamera
cards.explain: Without it, the renderer never builds a shadow map at all.

cards.title: How it works
cards.body:
The light "photographs" the scene from its own point of view into a depth texture, the shadow map. Then each pixel is checked: can the light see it? If not, it is in shadow.

The map size is light.shadow.mapSize (512×512 by default). Bigger is sharper, but costlier.

cards.q: Shadows look jagged and blurry. What do you try first?
options: Increase light.shadow.mapSize and tighten the shadow camera's area
cards.explain: A DirectionalLight renders shadows with an ortho camera, light.shadow.camera. The smaller its box, the sharper the result.

cards.q: Which lights can cast shadows? Select all that apply.
cards.explain: Ambient shines from everywhere, so there is no side to cast a shadow from. A PointLight renders six maps, which is expensive.

cards.q: Match each flag to its meaning
pairs: The light builds a shadow map

cards.q: The floor receives shadows
cards.code: floor.___ = true;
cards.explain: An object can both cast and receive: set both flags.

cards.task: From scratch: a shaded knot that casts a shadow on the floor, with a Lambert material.

cards.q: The scene is set up right and the camera points at the model, but the screen is black. The model uses MeshStandardMaterial. First guess?
cards.explain: Temporarily switch to MeshNormalMaterial or add an AmbientLight, and check.

cards.q: Which line is unnecessary for the knot's shadow?
cards.explain: AmbientLight casts no shadows: it has no direction.

cards.q: Match the symptom to the cause
pairs: Only Ambient, or a Basic material
One of the four flags is missing
Lamp does not reach from afar

cards.q: What makes a scene heavier for the GPU? Select all that apply.
cards.explain: Basic is the cheapest material there is.

cards.q: A smooth metal surface
cards.code: { metalness: ___, roughness: ___ }
cards.explain: And do not forget an environment map: metal needs something to reflect.

cards.q: What makes MeshStandardMaterial better than Lambert?
options: It is physically based: highlights, roughness, metal, and it matches glTF materials
cards.explain: Use Lambert when you want cheap and no highlights.

cards.task: Only ambient light, so the knot looks flat. Give it depth without touching the material.

units.title: Textures and models
units.blurb: TextureLoader, sRGB and repeating, loading glTF, centering and scaling a model, dispose. The course final.

cards.title: A picture on a surface
cards.body: A texture is an image wrapped onto geometry using UV coordinates. You load it with TextureLoader and put it into the material's map property.

cards.title: Why the colors look washed out
cards.body:
Regular images (JPG, PNG) store colors in the sRGB color space. Three.js does its lighting math in linear space. If you do not say the texture is sRGB, its colors are read as linear and come out pale and faded.

Only color maps get this flag (map, emissiveMap). Normal and roughness maps are data, so leave them alone.

cards.task: The tile should repeat 4×4 and have correct colors.

cards.q: repeat = 4, but instead of tiles you get one copy in the corner and stretched stripes. What is wrong?
options: wrapS and wrapT are set to ClampToEdge; repeating needs RepeatWrapping
cards.explain: By default the edges are "clamped": everything outside 0…1 takes the edge pixel.

cards.q: Which textures need colorSpace = SRGBColorSpace? Select all that apply.
cards.explain: Normals and roughness are numbers, not colors.

cards.q: An 8×8 tiling
cards.code:
tex.wrapS = tex.wrapT = THREE.___;
tex.repeat.set(___, 8);
cards.explain: MirroredRepeatWrapping repeats too, but mirrors every other copy.

cards.q: Match them up
You changed wrapS on a texture that is already on screen, and nothing happened. What do you do?
cards.explain: Some texture settings only take effect when the texture is uploaded to the GPU.

cards.title: glTF: the "JPEG of 3D"
cards.body: Ready-made models in Three.js are almost always loaded as glTF (.gltf or binary .glb): geometry, PBR materials, textures and animations in one file. The format itself is covered in the "3D formats" course.

cards.q: What do you add to the scene after loading?
options: gltf.scene, a group with all of the model's objects
cards.explain: gltf also has animations, cameras and asset; you take those separately.

cards.title: The model is huge, or off to one side
cards.body: Models arrive at all sorts of scales, with their center anywhere. A bounding box, Box3, helps you put the model in its place.

cards.q: Put the steps for showing a model in order
items: Move it to the center and fit the scale
Set up the lights and the camera
cards.explain: Without light, glTF's PBR materials will be black.

cards.title: Compressed models
cards.body: Heavy geometry is compressed with Draco or meshopt, which makes the file several times smaller. The loader needs a decoder:

cards.title: Removed from the scene ≠ memory freed
cards.body: scene.remove(model) only takes the object out of the scene. Geometry, materials and textures stay in GPU memory until you call dispose(). renderer.info.memory helps you spot a leak.

cards.q: A configurator swaps models, and after an hour the tab crashes. renderer.info.memory.geometries keeps growing. What is wrong?
options: Old models are removed from the scene, but dispose is never called
cards.explain: The JavaScript garbage collector does not free GPU memory.

cards.q: Where is the memory leak?
cards.explain: current was removed, but its geometry, materials and textures were never freed.

cards.q: Match them up

lessons.title: Course final
lessons.sub: A scene from empty canvas to loaded model

cards.task: Warm-up: a spinning cube from scratch.
Red and blue are visible, green is not. Show all three by only moving the camera back.
A shaded knot with a Standard material and a shadow.
The 4×4 tiling is already there, but the colors look washed out. Fix it.

cards.q: The order of a typical program
cards.explain: Plus a resize handler, which can go anywhere.

cards.q: Match the symptom to the fix
What comes from three/addons? Select all that apply.
cards.explain: Cameras, scenes and materials live in three itself.

cards.q: What comes next, at the intermediate level?
options: Environment maps and HDR, glTF animations, clicking on objects (Raycaster), InstancedMesh and performance
Nothing, that is all there is
cards.explain: Shaders, WebGPU and TSL come at the advanced level.
